I don’t see how disagreeing with you constitutes “a complete and utter lack of grasp of the subject”. That’s hyperbole.

So your claim is that the state of the art weather models are accurate at somewhere between 24h and 2 weeks (unclear based on the other sub threads) and continually improving. Based on this you extrapolate that given enough compute and sensors it would be possible to predict the weather with the same accuracy a month or more out. I think that’s a reasonable claim assuming that (1) the behavior of the system is deterministic and (2) the system behaves the same at both time scales.

Setting (1) aside, I claim that (2) is a wrong assumption. That weather exhibits chaotic behavior and that this likely puts an upper bound on prediction accuracy and the upper bound is less than 1 month.

The state of the art appears to be GraphCast [1] and FengWu [2]. These show promise out past 2 weeks when run against historical data. However, neither model is making actual weather predictions, and both are still in preprint (e.g. methodology has not been peer reviewed). This is super interesting and it’s possible my claim is incorrect, and that the upper bound is further out than the conventional 2 week limit.

author: 2ef0504e560d7088
comment_text:
Thanks, I haven't been able to give the paper a proper read, but are they're basing claims via results or the ability to recover physics equations?

Because those two things are very different. You can have models that make accurate predictions without having accurate models of "the world" (your environment, not necessarily the actual world)[0]. We can't meaningful call something a physics model (or a world model) without that counterfactual recovery (you don't need the exact laws of physics but you need something reasonable). After all, our physics equations are the most compressed forms or representing the information we're after.

I ask because this is a weird thing that happens in a lot of ML papers when approaching world models. But just looking at results isn't enough to conclude if a world is being modeled. Doesn't even tell you if that's self consistent, let alone counterfactual.

[0] classic example is the geocentric model. They made accurate predictions, which is why it stayed around for so long. It's not like the heliocentric model didn't present new problems. There was reason for legitimate scientific debate at the time but that context is easily lost to history.
story_title: Towards a Physics Foundation Model

author: af1950cd4ba2ff28
comment_text:
Don’t give up on TDD.

I’ve invested hundreds of hours in process and tooling, and can now ship major features with tests in record time with Claude Code.

You have to coach it in TDD - no matter how much you explain in CLAUDE.md. That’s part because “a test that fails because the code isn’t written yet” is conceptually very similar to “a test that passes without the code we’re about to write” and is also similar to “a test that asserts the code we’re about to write is not there”. You have to watch closely to make sure it produces the first thing.

Why does it keep getting confused? You can’t blame it really. When two things are conceptually similar, models need lots of examples to distinguish between them. If the set of samples is sparse the model is likely to jump the small distance from a concept to similar ones.

So, you have to accept this as how Claude 4 works, keep it on a short leash, keep reminding it that it must watch the test fail, ask it if the test failed for the right reason (not some setup issue), and THEN give it permission to write the code.

The result is two mirror copies of your feature or fix: code and tests.

Reviewing code and tests together is pleasant because they mirror one another. The tests forever ensure your feature works as described, no manual testing needed, no regressions. And the model knows all the tricks to make your tests really beautiful.

TDD is the check and balance missing from most people’s agentic software dev process.

The article isn't "facing off against scientific fact": my main objection to the article (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45294489) is that it's mostly explaining long-established, uncontroversial academic consensus (which forms the background of this paper), rather than the paper's contributions. That's like attributing "the inverse square law is a low-order approximation to the behaviour of gravity, rather accurate for relatively slow and light" to Albert Einstein's hit new paper "Die Feldgleichungen der Gravitation" (which in fact barely mentions that fact, because all readers are expected to already know it).

> The culture war topic of gay and trans rights is saturated with articles on topics just like this one.

That would be because "biological reality" is among the most popular talking points of anti-gay and anti-trans folk, but a fairly-obscure feature of reality aligns well with the main gay / trans rights ideological narratives, and people who discover this for the first time get all excited and decide to write a blog post about it.

If reality were a different way – if mammalian sexual dimorphism were as rigid and neat as is popularly asserted –, then I'm sure there'd be academics talking about how "ascribing magical significance to biological trivia, demanding that people constrain their behaviour based on something you need a microscope to identify, is fundamentally at odds with the ideals of liberty, equality, and fraternity" (or some such), and populists yelling about how science "proves" that clothing choices are constrained by "biological reality" (though we have that anyway), and the LGBT bloggers would blog about something else. In other words, appeals to biological reality are not why supporters of gay and trans rights believe in their causes: pointing out "hey, biological sex doesn't work like human genders anyway" is to them just a tool for telling narratives, which is why (even though I get why they're written) I get vaguely annoyed by those articles you complained about.

Given this, your assertions in this comment thread significantly annoy me. The only reason this kind of research has to do with "the culture wars" is because the culture wars have attempted to appropriate the topic, and have successfully constructed an association between the things in your mind. That association doesn't exist in the article, it doesn't exist in the paper, and perhaps it doesn't even exist in reality (the science is currently inconclusive). You're the one making this about "the culture wars". I would rather discuss the far more interesting science.

author: 2ef0504e560d7088
comment_text:
Residual connections create numerical stability with respect to the gradient and network updating. Look up the vanishing gradient problem. We wouldn't be able to build these deep networks without them.

It's easier to see looking at ReLU because you'll clearly get dead neurons, when the gradient hits 0 you can't recover.

This can also me mitigated by modem activation functions that are smooth but the other problem is that your gradient signal degrades as you move further down the network. Residuals help keep a stronger signal being able to propagate through the whole network. You can see this one if you run the numbers by hand for even not so deep of a network.

So just saying, "numerically stable" means lots of things...
